extracted.intended_audience: Patent practitioners (petitioners and patent owners), counsel, and parties participating in USPTO inter partes review, post-grant review, and covered business method review proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and procedural standards for instituting and conducting USPTO inter partes, post-grant, and covered business method patent review proceedings, including claim construction, petition content, service, filing date, preliminary responses, and institution thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard (broadest reasonable interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office adopts the 'broadest reasonable interpretation' standard for claim construction in inter partes review, post-grant review, and covered business method patent review proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard is consistent with AIA legislative history and long-standing USPTO and Federal Circuit practice; it applies to patentability determination proceedings and is the proper method for construing claims in those contexts (citations: NTP, Yamamoto, Phillips, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply claim construction standard throughout proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'broadest reasonable interpretation' standard must be applied throughout a proceeding when the Board determines whether to institute the review and when the Board determines patentability of any challenged patent claim and any new claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to challenged claims, new claims added under 35 U.S.C. 316(d)/326(d), claims from merged derivation proceedings, original/new/amended claims from merged reissue applications, and merged reexaminations; a single claim construction standard must be used to prevent inconsistencies and inefficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of patent owner statements under 35 U.S.C. 301(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office may consider written statements of the patent owner filed in court or the Office regarding claim scope, but such statements are limited under 35 U.S.C. 301(d) 'to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim' and do not mandate adoption of the district court standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory language does not set a claim construction standard nor require the Office to adopt district court claim construction; Office has discretion whether to consider such statements in an instituted review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner must set forth claim construction in petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners must identify how the challenged claim is to be construed in the petition (see § 42.104(b)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is intended to provide sufficient notice to the patent owner and assist the Board in analyzing how cited prior art meets claim limitations. Petitioners are not required to define every claim term but must state that terms take their ordinary and customary meaning and point out any claim term with a special meaning and its specification definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of ordinary and customary meaning for claim terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim term is presumed to take on its ordinary and customary meaning — the meaning it would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art — unless the specification provides a special definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words of the claim are given their plain meaning unless that plain meaning is inconsistent with the specification (citing In re Zletz, In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech Ctr.). Petitioners need not define every term, only identify special definitions where present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner claim construction limited to proceeding (no preclusive effect asserted)
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner’s claim construction is relevant only to the proceeding and the Office cannot prejudge the effect, if any, of the petitioner’s claim construction on other proceedings (e.g., district court litigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office cannot know whether a district court will consider or give weight to a petitioner’s claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative claim constructions permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules do not prohibit providing alternative claim constructions in a petition or in later-authorized filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may present alternative constructions where appropriate; revisions later in the process are allowed (subject to filing rules and authorization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to correct petition limited to clerical/typographical errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions to correct a petition without changing the filing date (§§ 42.104(c), 42.204(c), 42.304(c)) only allow correction for clerical or typographical mistakes; substantive mistakes cannot be corrected without changing the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding whether to grant a motion to correct, the Board will consider any substantial substantive effect, including any effect on the patent owner’s ability to file a preliminary response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service methods and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Service may be made electronically upon agreement of the parties, by EXPRESS MAIL® or by means at least as fast and reliable as EXPRESS MAIL®, and personal service is not required. The rules do not require serving a patent owner who is not of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner may additionally serve at any other address known likely to effect service; serving the last designated representative is sufficient if it matches the correspondence address of record (§§ 42.105, 42.205).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties may express preferred method for service (not mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each party may express a preferred method for service as part of mandatory notices, but the Office does not require such a preference to be specified in the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressing a preference is optional; rules permit agreement-based electronic service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing date — acceptance of minor deficiencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board generally will accord a filing date and accept minor deficiencies that do not impact the Board’s ability to determine whether to institute the review or the patent owner’s ability to file a preliminary response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners should still make every effort to complete petitions accurately. Some omissions/mistakes can affect institution (e.g., citing incorrect portion of a reference or omission of a challenged claim). The Board plans to process petitions and accord a filing date as soon as practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain omissions are not minor (failure to state precise relief requested)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to include the specific relief requested for each claim challenged is not considered a minor deficiency and cannot be cured without consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office refused to adopt a rule expressly allowing cure of such an omission without impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time to cure petition deficiencies
rubrics_metrics.description: In most situations, one month is sufficient for correcting deficiencies in a petition; if a longer period is needed, the petitioner may re-file a complete petition (no filing date is accorded for the initial incomplete petition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner bears responsibility to re-file if necessary; the Board may accept minor omissions but will not necessarily grant extended cure periods as a matter of right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary response deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owner preliminary response deadline extended from two months to three months (§§ 42.107(b), 42.207(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owners may expedite by filing earlier or waive the preliminary response to speed the proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimonial evidence not allowed in preliminary response before institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owners are not permitted to submit new testimonial evidence with their preliminary response prior to institution; testimonial evidence by patent owners is permitted only after institution under the AIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing testimonial evidence pre-institution would likely require cross-examination and delay institution; patent owners wishing to submit such evidence pre-institution must seek authorization via motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-testimonial evidence and attorney arguments in preliminary response
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owner preliminary response may include evidence other than new testimonial evidence; however, attorney arguments are not evidence and cannot replace factually supported objective evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations to case law (In re Huang, In re De Blauwe) emphasize that arguments of counsel are not a substitute for evidence. A party seeking dismissal must seek authorization for a motion to dismiss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensions of time require authorization and proof of entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may seek authorization to file a motion seeking an extension of time; the moving party carries the burden of proving entitlement to relief (§ 42.20(a)-(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a motion is authorized or granted depends on the particular facts presented and is decided case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: No petitioner reply as of right prior to institution
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutes provide only a petition and a patent owner preliminary response prior to institution; petitioners do not have a right to reply prior to institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing a reply as of right would negatively affect the Office's ability to meet statutory time requirements (35 U.S.C. 314(b) and 324(c)). Parties can seek authorization for additional filings where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of institution decisions (claim-by-claim and ground-by-ground)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may authorize review to proceed on all or some of the challenged claims and on all or some of the grounds of unpatentability asserted for each claim (§§ 42.108(a), 42.208(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institution is a threshold decision and can be limited to particular claims/grounds for which the required statutory threshold is met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution thresholds: 'reasonable likelihood' and 'more likely than not'
rubrics_metrics.description: Review will not be instituted unless the Board decides that the petition would demonstrate a 'reasonable likelihood' (inter partes review) or 'more likely than not' (post-grant review) that at least one of the claims is unpatentable (35 U.S.C. 314(a)/324(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a petitioner meets the threshold is evaluated case-by-case. 'Reasonable likelihood' is a lower threshold than 'more likely than not'. The Office declines to further define beyond following statutory language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 35 U.S.C. 325(d) to deny repetitive or cumulative petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office will exercise its authority under 35 U.S.C. 325(d), where appropriate, to deny petitions that submit the same or substantially the same prior art or arguments previously presented to the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is intended to discourage piecemeal or successive petitions aimed at avoiding estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declining institution for inability to complete timely or for extreme complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office may decline to institute a proceeding where it determines it could not complete the proceeding timely or where the petition seeks review that is unmanageably large or complex (e.g., several hundred claims, a thousand references, or need for many foreign depositions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may take into account the Office's ability to timely complete the review as part of the considerations under 35 U.S.C. 316(b) and 326(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of a ground is a final Board decision; decision to institute is not reviewable
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may deny a ground at any time prior to institution; denial of a ground is a final Board decision subject to reconsideration at that time (§ 42.71(c)(2)). The Director’s decision on whether to institute review is not reviewable (35 U.S.C. 314(d), 324(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should be aware of the limited reviewability of institution decisions and the finality of ground denials for purposes of reconsideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service on other addresses known likely to effect service
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner may additionally serve the petition and supporting evidence on the patent owner at any other address known to the petitioner as likely to effect service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serving on the correspondence address of record is consistent with current practice (§ 41.106(e)); doing so helps ensure service when the patent owner of record may not be the practical recipient.
